extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television fans, media researchers, and students looking for an encyclopedia overview of The Cosby Show
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic entry summarizing the production, premise, episodes, cast, reception, awards, syndication history, and legacy of an American television sitcom (The Cosby Show).

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosby wanted the program to be educational, reflecting his own background in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes this guiding aim influenced production choices (e.g., storylines addressing dyslexia and teenage pregnancy) and the creator's insistence on certain production particulars such as taping in New York City rather than Los Angeles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of a successful, stable Black family
rubrics_metrics.description: The show's portrayal of a successful, stable black family was praised by some for breaking racial stereotypes and showing another part of the African-American experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as a central evaluative quality of the series' social significance; the article also records criticism that the portrayal could allow white audiences to think racism and poverty were problems of the past (e.g., Henry Louis Gates Jr.'s critique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to race and racial issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the cast and characters were predominantly African-American, issues of race were rarely mentioned compared to other contemporary African-American-led sitcoms; nonetheless the show frequently promoted African-American culture and culture of Africa via artists and musicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry contrasts The Cosby Show's restrained direct engagement with race against series that dealt more overtly with racial issues (e.g., The Jeffersons, and the spin-off A Different World which addressed race more often).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: blending comedy with serious subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite its comedic tone, the show sometimes involves serious subjects, like Theo's experiences dealing with dyslexia and teenage pregnancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are given (Theo's dyslexia inspired by Cosby's son Ennis; Denise's friend's pregnancy) showing the program's willingness to incorporate substantive social/health/education topics within a sitcom format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting and character design to convey aspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept was changed so that the family was well-off financially, with the mother a lawyer and the father a physician, to express the accomplishment of successfully raising a child who had graduated from college.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents the creators' deliberate choices about family status and professions as part of the show's messaging; it also records casting considerations (e.g., who was considered for Sondra and Denise) as part of shaping character identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production location and filming choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Cosby insisted that the program be taped in New York City instead of Los Angeles; early episodes were videotaped at NBC's Brooklyn studios, later moving to Kaufman Astoria Studios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry outlines how location choices (studio, exterior brownstone) and pilot-vs-series set differences were part of the show's production identity and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry success metrics (ratings and awards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cosby Show spent five consecutive seasons as television’s top-rated show and is one of only two sitcoms in Nielsen ratings history to finish at number one for five seasons; it accrued numerous awards (Emmys, Golden Globes, NAACP Image Awards, Peabody) and substantial revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article provides season-by-season Nielsen rankings and HH ratings, lists awards won and nominations, and cites syndication and revenue figures (e.g., $2.5 billion total television revenue) as concrete measures of success and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural impact and legacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The series helped make possible a larger variety of shows with predominantly black casts, created the 'Clair Huxtable effect' (influence on portrayal of working mothers), and made Cliff Huxtable an iconic figure ('America's Dad').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry documents spin-offs (A Different World), international popularity, influence on fashion (the 'Cosby sweaters'), and later rankings on 'best of' lists as ways the show's cultural legacy is assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical reputation affecting distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2014, reruns of The Cosby Show have been pulled from several networks and venues as a result of the Bill Cosby sexual assault cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article details which networks pulled the show (TV Land, Aspire, BET's Centric, Bounce TV, etc.), temporary resumptions, and subsequent removals (e.g., after Cosby's 2018 conviction), illustrating how off-screen ethical/legal issues altered the show's availability and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual identity and iconography (the 'Cosby sweater')
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliff Huxtable frequently wore colorful knit sweaters that became fashion trends and were dubbed 'Cosby sweaters'—a term used to describe sweaters perceived as garish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entry notes cultural references, erroneous attributions (Coogi vs. Koos Van Den Akker), auctions of the sweaters, and how the wardrobe contributed to the show's recognizable image.
